extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition of the fundamental principles, notation, and distinctions used in logical inference and the philosophy of science (substitution, induction vs. deduction, symbolic notation, terms and classes, relations). Explains how to represent and manipulate propositions symbolically and when substitution-based inferences are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: The one supreme rule of inference: Substitution of Similars
rubrics_metrics.description: The one supreme rule of inference consists in the direction to affirm of anything whatever is known of its like, equal or equivalent. (Phrase used: 'The Substitution of Similars')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From A = B and a relation between B and C, infer the same relation between A and C. The text stresses investigating when a degree of similarity less than complete identity suffices for substitution and gives many examples (weights, measures, fragments, tones, species). It emphasizes that substitution underlies deduction, induction, analogy, classification, and quantitative reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: General formula of logical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: General symbolic formula: from A = B :<>: C we may infer A (relation) C — i.e., whatever relation a thing stands to a second thing, in the same relation it stands to the like or equivalent of that second thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: if C is weight of B then C is weight of A; if C is father of B then C is father of A; fragment/quality/species examples. Guidance includes that substitution can be applied to parts of aggregates and complex wholes (same parts samely related make same wholes). Also shows replacement can be repeated indefinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction and interdependence of Deduction and Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction: passing from more general to less general truths (developing consequences of a law). Induction: from less to more general truths (discovering the law from observed consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although all knowledge is derived by induction from experience, the text argues that induction requires prior knowledge of deduction — induction is the inverse of deduction. Importance of mastering deductive processes to understand and perform induction is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance and role of symbolic expression in logic
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear, brief, and appropriate system of symbols is almost essential to express the general truths of logic and science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs required: symbols for terms, for sameness (=), for difference (-), and for conjunctions/relations. Blank letters (A, B, C, etc.) are recommended to represent undetermined or unknown terms. Symbolic language helps exhibit the general form of reasoning disentangled from subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and broadened meaning of the '=' sign (identity/equivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt '=' to denote some form or degree of sameness; the particular form is indicated by the nature of the terms joined by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains historical usage and extension beyond mathematical equality to equivalence of operations, logical identity, and equivalence of meaning (philology, chemistry). Cautions to distinguish identity from inclusion/partial identity (e.g., 'is' can be ambiguous). Gives examples (Hydrogen = least dense element; Exogenous plants = Dicotyledons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for negative terms (Not A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative or 'not' terms denote objects that do not possess the whole of the qualities assigned to a positive term; recommend a briefer symbol for Not A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following De Morgan, negative terms may be represented by small Roman or italic letters (a, b, c ...), where a denotes 'not A'. Example: if A means 'fluid', then a means 'not fluid'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol to denote difference or general relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '-' (introduced by Wallis) to signify difference; use a general relation sign (cos / c//i) to signify any relation between two terms (equality, inequality, time, place, size, causation, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: B - C denotes B and C are not identical; A cos B can denote any conceivable relation. This provides flexibility to express varied logical relations beyond simple identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same parts samely related make same wholes (axiom)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general axiom: same parts samely related make same wholes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: building two houses from exactly similar bricks similarly placed gives similar houses; replacing a weight in a balance by its equivalent preserves equilibrium; substitution is the general test of equality for brightness, dimensions, etc. Emphasizes substitution as the general test for equality and similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagating power of similarity and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity propagates among things made similar to the same standard; standards and accurate copies guarantee mutual agreement among copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: coins struck from same dies, printed copies from same type, tuning-forks adjusted to a standard, standard measures of length/weight. Explains practical value in manufacturing (interchangeable parts) and measurement propagation ad infinitum if copies are accurately executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms: concrete, abstract, and classes; logical abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms denote objects and usually imply possession of certain qualities; abstraction allows thinking of qualities separately and forming abstract terms/classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses progression from concrete single objects to abstract notions (e.g. 'hardness of a flower'), formation of classes by grouping objects that share a quality, and the mental operation of treating objects as aggregates of qualities. Emphasizes the need to decide safely how far to assign an object to a class when reasoning about general names.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Logic of Relatives (relations of time and space require special treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations of time and space and other relative relations (e.g., familial relations) form a difficult branch of logic requiring special treatment; simple syllogistic forms may not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives example: to infer Daniel is nephew of James requires assuming rules about 'son of a brother'. References Peirce, De Morgan, Ellis, Harley for notation and treatments of relatives; warns of abstract/difficult investigation needed for these relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in choosing mode of expression vs. metaphysical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer exhibiting truths in a clear and formal manner rather than engaging in metaphysical discussion over terms (e.g., noun vs adjective distinctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters may be used indifferently for nouns substantive and adjectives; grammatical usage permits conversion of adjectives into substantives for clarity in formal exposition. The author focuses on formal, exhibit-able truths rather than metaphysics.
